In 1832 the Federal Diet decided on a common **Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer** for Catholic and Reformed places. It is celebrated on the third Sunday in September and today is often arranged in an interreligious way. In 1992 the Interreligious Working Group **IRAS COTIS** was founded. After **catastrophes and accidents**, several religious communities often arrange memorial services together. In this way all those affected can mourn in their own tradition.

gewusst: IRAS COTIS is today supported by about 70 religious communities and organisations.
The day of prayer is one of the oldest shared holidays of the Confederation.

teile.einleitung: In Buddhism, a bodhisattva is a being who strives for enlightenment in order to help all living beings. The bodhisattva ideal is especially important in Mahayana Buddhism, which is widespread in China, Japan, Korea and Tibet.
wichtigste: Bodhisattva literally means “enlightenment being”.
Mahayana contrasts the bodhisattva with the arhat, who mainly seeks his own liberation.
The resolve to become enlightened for the good of all beings is called bodhicitta.
The classic list names six perfections, the paramitas.
Avalokiteshvara is the bodhisattva of compassion; in China he is called Guanyin.
Maitreya is regarded as the future Buddha.

abschnitte.text: The word **bodhisattva** is made up of two parts: **bodhi** means awakening or enlightenment, and **sattva** means being. A bodhisattva strives to become a Buddha. But he does this not only for himself, but for the **good of all living beings**. That is why, according to the teaching, he postpones his final passing away in order to help others.

In older Buddhism, the **arhat** was an important model. The arhat reaches his own liberation. In **Mahayana**, the “great vehicle”, this goal was regarded as too limited. There the bodhisattva, who wants to help everyone, is at the centre. The path begins with **bodhicitta**, the “mind of enlightenment”: the firm resolve to become enlightened for the good of all.

On his path the bodhisattva practises the **paramitas**, the perfections. The classic Mahayana list names six: **generosity**, **ethical conduct**, **patience**, **energy**, **meditation** and **wisdom**. Later lists extend them to ten. The Indian monk **Shantideva** described this path in the 8th century in his work **Bodhicaryavatara**, which is very popular in Tibetan Buddhism.

**Avalokiteshvara** is the bodhisattva of **compassion**. In China he is usually shown as female, as **Guanyin**, and in Japan the figure is called **Kannon**. **Manjushri** embodies **wisdom** and often holds a flaming sword that cuts through ignorance. **Maitreya** is regarded in all the major schools as the **future Buddha**. His name is connected with the word for kindness.

gewusst: In Tibetan Buddhism, the Dalai Lama is regarded as an embodiment of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara.
According to tradition, Maitreya waits in the Tushita heaven until he is born as the next Buddha.

teile.einleitung: In the **dragon dance**, many people carry a long, colourful dragon made of cloth through the streets. They move it so that it winds along as if it were alive. In China the dance belongs above all to the New Year festival.
wichtigste: Many people carry a dragon together.
The dancers hold the dragon up on poles.
In China the dragon stands for good fortune and strength.
The dragon often chases a ball, the “pearl”.
Drums and cymbals accompany the dance.
The dragon dance is often seen at Chinese New Year.

abschnitte.text: In many European fairy tales the dragon is a dangerous monster. In **China** it is quite different. There the dragon is a good being. It stands for **good fortune**, **strength** and wisdom. In the past it was also the emperor’s emblem. People believed that dragons bring rain for the fields.

The dragon has a big head and a long body made of cloth. **Poles** are fixed under the body. Each dancer holds one pole and so moves one piece of the dragon. Everyone must work together exactly so that the dragon waves and leaps beautifully. At the front, one person carries a **ball** on a pole. The dragon chases this “pearl” and twists back and forth.

Loud music belongs to the dragon dance. **Drums**, **cymbals** and gongs set the beat. The dancers move in time with the rhythm. According to old belief, the noise is also meant to drive away evil spirits. Often firecrackers go off as well.

The dragon dance is seen most often at **Chinese New Year**, which begins in January or February. People also dance at other festivals and openings. It is said: the **longer** the dragon, the **more good fortune** it brings. Some dragons are very long and are carried by dozens of people. There are dragon dances in cities outside China too, where many Chinese people live.

gewusst: The dragon dance is not the same as the lion dance: in the lion dance there are usually only two people inside a lion costume.
The dragon is also one of the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac.

teile.einleitung: The Inuit live in the Arctic, in Greenland, Canada and Alaska. Their old beliefs tell of spirits in the sea, the air and animals. Many of these stories were passed on orally and only written down later.
wichtigste: The Inuit live in Greenland, in the north of Canada and in Alaska.
Sedna is the sea goddess; she rules over the sea creatures.
According to the myth, seals, walruses and whales arose from her fingers.
The shaman is called an angakkuq.
Sila is the force of air, weather and the order of the world.
Knud Rasmussen wrote down many myths on the Fifth Thule Expedition.
In 1721 the missionary Hans Egede came to Greenland.

abschnitte.text: The most important figure in many tales is **Sedna**. According to belief she lives on the sea floor and rules over all sea creatures. According to one myth she plunged into the sea and her fingers were cut off. From the finger joints came **seals, walruses and whales**. When Sedna is angry, she holds the animals back, and the hunters find no prey.

The Inuit believed that many forces work in nature. **Sila** stands for air, weather and the order of the world. The word also means reason. According to this belief, animals also have a soul. That is why hunters often gave a killed seal a sip of **fresh water**, because seals are thirsty in salt water. In this way they honoured the soul of the animal and hoped for further luck in hunting.

The shaman is called an **angakkuq**. According to belief, the angakkuq could travel to the spirits, for example to Sedna on the sea floor. He was to heal the sick and put right wrongs when someone had broken a **taboo**. A taboo is a rule that must not be broken. The angakkuq was thus a very important person in the community.

For the dancing **northern lights** in the sky there were explanations of their own. In many regions people believed that the souls of the dead were playing ball there. In Greenland people told of the **tupilaq**, a magical figure made of bone and fur that was meant to harm an enemy. Today artists carve small tupilaq figures from bone or stone. They are popular works of art.

The explorer **Knud Rasmussen** travelled from 1921 to 1924 on the Fifth Thule Expedition with dog sledges from Greenland to Alaska. On the way he wrote down many stories and songs of the Inuit. As early as 1721 the Norwegian pastor **Hans Egede** had come to Greenland. He founded the settlement that later became Nuuk. After that Christianity spread, and the old forms of belief receded.

gewusst: According to belief, seals are thirsty because they always live in salt water.
Nuuk, today’s capital of Greenland, goes back to the settlement of Hans Egede.

teile.einleitung: Dao is a central concept of Chinese thought. The word means “way”. In Daoism it refers to the origin and natural order of all things.
wichtigste: Dao (also Tao) literally means “way”.
The Daodejing begins with the statement that the Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao.
Qi is the life energy that flows through people and nature.
Taijiquan is a slow martial art connected with Daoism.
Zhuangzi dreamed that he was a butterfly.
A Daoist temple is often called a “guan” in Chinese.

abschnitte.text: **Dao**, also written **Tao**, literally means “**way**”. In **Daoism** it refers to the origin and the order of all things. The most important book of Daoism, the **Daodejing**, begins with the sentence: “The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao.” This makes it clear that the Dao cannot be fully captured in words.

Daoism teaches that one should live **in harmony with nature**. You follow the natural order and live simply. Anyone who goes against the course of things loses their strength. Closely connected with this is the idea of **yin and yang**: two opposites such as light and shadow that belong together.

In Chinese thought, a life force flows through people and nature. It is called **qi**, also written chi. Exercises such as **qigong** are meant to strengthen it. The slow martial art **taijiquan**, often called tai chi, consists of flowing movements. It is based on yin and yang and the harmonious flow of qi. There are many courses for it in Switzerland too.

After **Laozi**, **Zhuangzi** is regarded as the most important thinker of Daoism. A famous story tells that he dreamed he was a **butterfly**. When he woke up, he asked himself: am I a man who dreamed he was a butterfly? Or a butterfly who is dreaming that he is a man? The story invites us to think about dreams and reality.

Daoist temples are often called “**guan**” in Chinese. A well-known example is the **Baiyun Guan**, the White Cloud Temple in **Beijing**. Daoist **monks** also live there. They pray, meditate and look after old writings and customs.

gewusst: The well-known black and white yin-yang symbol is called the taijitu in Chinese.
In China, many older people practise taijiquan together in parks early in the morning.

teile.einleitung: The word **diaspora** comes from Greek and means “scattering”. It refers mainly to Jews who live outside the land of Israel. The Jewish diaspora is over 2,500 years old and has produced languages, customs and communities all over the world.
wichtigste: Diaspora means “scattering”.
After the conquest of Jerusalem, many Jews lived in the Babylonian Exile until the Persian king Cyrus II allowed them to return in 539 BC.
In antiquity, Alexandria in Egypt had a very large Jewish community.
Ashkenazim come from Central and Eastern Europe, Sephardim from Spain and Portugal.
In 1492 the Jews were expelled from Spain.
Immigration to Israel is called aliyah.
Outside Israel, most Jews today live in the USA.

abschnitte.text: In the 6th century BC, the Babylonians conquered Jerusalem and took many Jews to Babylon. This **Babylonian Exile** ended when the Persian king **Cyrus II** conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed them to return home. But many stayed in the east and founded communities there. Jewish settlements also arose around the Mediterranean. Especially many Jews lived in **Alexandria**. There the **Septuagint** came into being, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.

In the Middle Ages, two large groups formed. The **Ashkenazim** lived first on the Rhine and later mainly in Eastern Europe. Their language was **Yiddish**, which arose from Middle High German and is written in Hebrew letters. The **Sephardim** lived in Spain and Portugal. After the **Alhambra Decree** of 1492, the Jews had to leave Spain. Many moved to North Africa and the Ottoman Empire.

In many countries, Jews had fewer rights than other people for a long time. In **Venice**, from 1516 they had to live in an enclosed district. All later **ghettos** are named after this district. In Switzerland too, Jews were for a long time allowed to live in only a few places, such as Endingen and Lengnau in Aargau. In the 20th century, the National Socialists murdered about six million Jews in the **Shoah**.

The Hebrew word **galut** means exile. Unlike the neutral word diaspora, it stresses life far from the promised land as a state of lack. Since the founding of the State of Israel in 1948, millions of Jews have immigrated. This immigration is called **aliyah**, which means “ascent”. Even so, about half of all Jews still live in the diaspora today. The largest community outside Israel lives in the **USA**.

gewusst: Before the Second World War, Yiddish was the everyday language of millions of people in Eastern Europe.
In the Middle Ages, “Ashkenaz” was the Hebrew name for Germany and “Sepharad” the one for Spain.
Today people also speak of a diaspora among other peoples, for example the Armenians or the Tibetans.

teile.einleitung: Augusta Raurica was a Roman town on the Rhine, east of Basel. Its remains lie in the present-day municipalities of Augst and Kaiseraugst. Here you can discover a theatre, temples and many finds from Roman times.
wichtigste: Augusta Raurica lies in Augst (Basel-Landschaft) and Kaiseraugst (Aargau).
The town lay directly on the Rhine.
Lucius Munatius Plancus mentions a founding in 44 BC.
The site was only permanently settled around 15 BC.
In the sanctuary in the Grienmatt, a god of healing was worshipped.
The Schönbühl temple stood opposite the theatre.

abschnitte.titel: A Roman town on the Rhine
abschnitte.text: **Augusta Raurica** lay directly on the Rhine. Its remains are today in **Augst** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft and **Kaiseraugst** in the canton of Aargau. The name recalls Emperor Augustus and the **Rauraci**, a Celtic tribe. The town was an important place for trade and traffic. Today Augusta Raurica is one of the largest Roman sites in Switzerland.

The Roman **Lucius Munatius Plancus** mentions in his tomb inscription the founding of a colony in the territory of the Rauraci. His tomb stands in Gaeta in Italy. The founding is dated there to **44 BC**. But Augusta Raurica was only permanently settled around **15 BC**. After that the town grew into an important centre.

The inhabitants worshipped many gods. In the sanctuary in the **Grienmatt** there was a healing bath and an altar to **Aesculapius Augustus**. The name links the god of healing, Aesculapius, with the emperor. Typical of the region are **Gallo-Roman temples with an ambulatory**: a square inner room, the cella, with a passage all the way round. This style of building combines Celtic tradition with Roman technique.

On a hill opposite the theatre stood the **Schönbühl temple**. It was a podium temple in the Roman style, that is, built on a high base. Theatre and temple formed a common axis. The **theatre** is well preserved and is used again for performances today. Every summer a big Roman festival also takes place.

gewusst: In Kaiseraugst, a large Roman silver treasure was found in 1961.
In the reconstructed Roman house in Augst you can see how a Roman family lived.

teile.einleitung: Noah’s Ark is a large ship from a well-known story in the Bible. Noah builds it to save his family and the animals from a mighty flood. At the end, a dove with an olive branch shows that the flood is over.
wichtigste: The story is in the first book of the Bible, Genesis.
At God’s command, Noah builds a huge ship, the ark.
He takes his family and animals of every kind with him.
According to the Bible, it rains for 40 days and 40 nights.
The ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
A dove brings back an olive branch.
The rainbow is the sign of God’s promise.

abschnitte.text: The story is in the **first book of Moses**, Genesis. God is disappointed because people do so much evil. Only **Noah** is regarded as righteous. God commands him to build a large ship of wood, the **ark**. The word “ark” means a chest or box.

Noah goes into the ark with his wife, his three sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and their wives. He also takes animals of every kind with him, so that they can go on living after the flood. Then it begins to rain. According to the Bible, it rains for **40 days and 40 nights**. The water rises so high that even the mountains are covered.

When the rain stops, the ark comes to rest on the mountains of **Ararat**. Noah first sends out a raven and then a **dove**. On the second flight, the dove comes back with a fresh **olive branch** in its beak. From this Noah knows that trees are growing again and the flood is over. That is why the dove with the branch is still a sign of peace today.

After the flood, Noah, his family and the animals leave the ark. God promises never to send such a flood again. As a sign of this covenant, he sets the **rainbow** in the sky. Similar flood stories exist in other ancient cultures too, for example in the **Epic of Gilgamesh** from Mesopotamia. In the Koran too, Noah is mentioned as a prophet, where he is called Nuh.

gewusst: The dove of peace with the olive branch goes back to the story of Noah.
Ararat is a high volcanic mountain in the east of Turkey.

teile.einleitung: In interreligious dialogue, people of different religions talk with one another. They want to understand one another better and live together peacefully. Nobody has to give up their own faith in doing so.
wichtigste: The aim is for religions to understand one another and live together peacefully.
Cooperation among Christian churches is called ecumenism.
In 1893 the first World Parliament of Religions met in Chicago.
In 1986 Pope John Paul II invited people to Assisi for a prayer for peace.
Hans Küng from Sursee founded the Global Ethic project.
In Switzerland, the Week of Religions has been held every year at the beginning of November since 2007.

abschnitte.text: In **interreligious dialogue**, members of different religions learn from one another. They tell of their faith, their festivals and their values. In this way they break down **prejudices**. Nobody has to give up their own faith in doing so. Cooperation between different Christian churches, by contrast, is called **ecumenism**. Dialogue between different religions is called interreligious.

In 1893 the first **World Parliament of Religions** met in **Chicago**. It is regarded as the beginning of modern interreligious dialogue. In 1986 Pope **John Paul II** invited representatives of many religions to **Assisi**, the city of Saint Francis. A world day of prayer for peace took place there. Since then there have been several such meetings there.

abschnitte.titel: Hans Küng and the Global Ethic
abschnitte.text: The theologian **Hans Küng** came from **Sursee** in the canton of Lucerne. He lived from 1928 to 2021. In 1990 he presented the **Global Ethic project**. He wanted to find common values that hold in all the great religions, such as honesty and respect for life. His guiding thought was that there can be no peace among nations without peace among religions.

The Interreligious Working Group in Switzerland, **IRAS COTIS**, created the **Week of Religions** and coordinates it. It has been held every year since 2007 at the **beginning of November**. All over Switzerland there are then meetings, visits and events. In 2006 the **Swiss Council of Religions** was founded. On it sit representatives of Christian churches and of Jewish and Muslim associations.

gewusst: Many school classes in Switzerland visit a mosque, a synagogue or a temple during the Week of Religions.
Hans Küng taught for many years at the University of Tübingen in Germany.

teile.einleitung: The **Día de los Muertos**, the “Day of the Dead”, is a major festival in **Mexico**. Families remember their dead, but not sadly: with colours, music and food. People believe that the dead come to visit on these days.
wichtigste: The festival is celebrated mainly on 1 and 2 November.
The decorated altar at home is called an ofrenda.
Orange marigolds are meant to show the dead the way.
People give skulls made of sugar and bake pan de muerto.
The figure “La Catrina” goes back to José Guadalupe Posada.
UNESCO counts the Day of the Dead as intangible cultural heritage.

abschnitte.text: The **Aztecs** and other peoples of Mexico already honoured their dead with festivals. According to their belief, many of the dead went to **Mictlan**, the underworld. When the Spanish came, they brought Christianity with them. The old customs merged with the Christian holy days of **All Saints’ Day** and **All Souls’ Day** on 1 and 2 November. That is how today’s festival came about.

In many homes people build an **ofrenda**, a decorated altar. On it stand photos of the dead, candles, and their favourite foods and drinks. Bright orange **marigolds**, called cempasúchil in Spanish, are added. Their colour and scent are meant to show the dead the way home. Many families also decorate the graves and spend time at the cemetery.

Typical are brightly decorated **skulls made of sugar**, the calaveras. A person’s name is often written on them, and they are given as gifts. For the festival people bake **pan de muerto**, a sweet bread. It is often decorated with strips of dough that look like bones. The skulls are not meant to be scary, but cheerful.

At the beginning of the 20th century, the Mexican artist **José Guadalupe Posada** drew a skeleton of an elegant lady with a big hat. From this came the famous figure **“La Catrina”**. She shows that in death everyone is equal, whether rich or poor. Today many people dress up as Catrina and paint their faces. **UNESCO** added the Day of the Dead to the List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

gewusst: The painter Diego Rivera later gave the figure the name “Catrina”.
The Día de los Muertos is a different festival from Halloween, even though the two take place at almost the same time.

teile.einleitung: A prayer mat is a small carpet on which Muslims pray. Because you should pray in a clean place, many Muslims spread out their own mat. It is among the most important objects in the everyday life of many Muslims.
wichtigste: Many Muslims kneel on a prayer mat to pray.
Prayer takes place in a clean place.
Muslims pray five times a day.
In prayer they turn towards Mecca.
On many prayer mats a prayer niche is shown.

abschnitte.text: In **Islam**, believers pray five times a day at fixed times. The prayer is called **salat**. For it you should pray in a **clean place**. That is why many Muslims spread out their own **prayer mat**. In this way they can pray anywhere, at home, at work or on a journey. Before the prayer they also wash their hands, face and feet.

In prayer, Muslims turn towards the city of **Mecca** in Saudi Arabia. There stands the **Kaaba**, the most important sanctuary of Islam. The mat is laid so that its upper end points towards Mecca. On many prayer mats a **prayer niche** is shown, like those found in mosques. Today a **compass** or an app often helps to find the direction.

In prayer you first stand, then bow, kneel and touch the ground with your **forehead**. The mat protects against dirt and cold. You step onto the prayer mat **without shoes**. After the prayer it is usually rolled or folded up and put in a clean place. People take care not to walk about on it carelessly.

Prayer mats come in many colours and patterns. They often show ornaments, flowers or pictures of mosques. People and animals are usually not shown on them. Some mats are hand knotted and very precious, others are simple and light for travelling. In a **mosque** there is usually a large carpet for everyone, so you do not need your own there.

gewusst: In Arabic the prayer mat is called “sajjada”; the word is connected with prostrating oneself in prayer.
There are prayer mats with a built-in compass, so that you can find the direction of Mecca even when travelling.

teile.einleitung: Jewish emancipation means that Jews receive the same rights as everyone else. In Europe this happened step by step in the 18th and 19th centuries. In Switzerland the vote of 1866 and the constitution of 1874 were decisive.
wichtigste: In 1791 France was the first country in Europe to make Jews legally equal.
The Federal Constitution of 1848 gave freedom of settlement only to Swiss of Christian denomination.
On 14 January 1866, the people and the cantons approved freedom of settlement for Jews.
Of nine proposals, only this one was accepted in 1866.
Full freedom of belief and worship came with the Federal Constitution of 1874.
In 1860 only about 4,000 Jews lived in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Emancipation** means liberation and equal status. For a long time Jews in many countries were not allowed to live freely, to practise every trade or to have full civil rights. In 1791, in the course of the revolution, **France** was the first country in Europe to make all Jews completely equal in law. The example influenced many other countries. In other states, however, equal status often took decades more.

In the Old Swiss Confederacy, Jews were for a long time allowed to live only in two villages in Aargau: **Endingen and Lengnau**. The Federal Constitution of 1848 gave freedom of settlement in **Article 41** only to Swiss of Christian denomination. Jews were thus excluded from free settlement. According to the census of 1860, only about **4,000** Jews lived in the country, about 0.2 per cent of the population.

The disadvantage bothered other states. In 1863 the **Netherlands** refused a trade treaty because it would have disadvantaged their Jewish citizens. France and the USA also applied pressure. The **settlement treaty with France** of 1864 allowed French Jews free settlement in Switzerland. Swiss Jews would thus have been worse off than foreign ones.

On **14 January 1866**, the people and the cantons voted on nine changes to the Federal Constitution. Only one found a majority: **freedom of settlement** for non-Christians. With about 53 per cent yes, the result was narrow, and 12½ cantons agreed. Geneva and Neuchâtel said yes with over 85 per cent. That is why people speak of the “only yes of 1866”.

In 1866 it was only about settlement and equality before the law. Only the totally revised **Federal Constitution of 1874** guaranteed general **freedom of belief and worship**. At municipal level, some still hesitated. In Aargau the Jews of Endingen and Lengnau received local citizenship only in **1879**. With that they were full citizens in their own villages too.

gewusst: Of nine proposals on 14 January 1866, only freedom of settlement was accepted.
Trade treaties with other countries helped Swiss Jews to receive equal rights.

teile.einleitung: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was an Indian lawyer, politician and social reformer. He fought against the caste system all his life and led the committee that drew up the constitution of independent India.
wichtigste: Ambedkar was born in 1891 into a Mahar family, who were regarded as “untouchable”.
He earned a doctorate at Columbia University in New York and also studied in London.
He led the committee that drew up the Indian constitution; it came into force on 26 January 1950.
Article 17 of the constitution abolishes untouchability.
In 1936 he wrote the text “Annihilation of Caste” against the caste system.
In 1956 he converted to Buddhism in Nagpur together with hundreds of thousands of Dalits.

abschnitte.text: Ambedkar was born in **1891**. His family belonged to the **Mahar**, a group regarded as “untouchable”. Today these people are called **Dalits**. Even at school, Ambedkar experienced serious discrimination: for example, he was not allowed to sit next to other children. Even so, he studied very hard.

Ambedkar studied at **Columbia University** in New York and earned a doctorate there. After that he studied at the **London School of Economics**. He became a lawyer and an economist. This made him one of the best-educated politicians of his time. He used his knowledge for the rights of the Dalits.

Ambedkar demanded equal rights for all. On 25 December 1927 he publicly burned the **Manusmriti**, an old law book that in his view justified untouchability. In 1932 he argued with **Gandhi** about the political representation of the Dalits. Ambedkar wanted separate electorates, while Gandhi was against it and fasted. In the **Poona Pact** they agreed on reserved seats. In 1936 his text “**Annihilation of Caste**” appeared, in which he demanded the abolition of the castes.

After India’s independence in 1947, Ambedkar became the first **Minister of Law and Justice**. He led the committee that drew up the **constitution**. It came into force on **26 January 1950**. **Article 17** forbids untouchability in every form and makes it a punishable offence. That is why Ambedkar is often called the “father of the constitution” in India.

Ambedkar was looking for a religion without a caste order. On **14 October 1956** he converted to **Buddhism** in **Nagpur**. Hundreds of thousands of Dalits did the same. A few weeks later, in December 1956, he died. To this day he is a great role model for many Dalits.

gewusst: 26 January, the day the constitution came into force, is now a national holiday in India, “Republic Day”.
In many Indian villages and towns there are statues of Ambedkar, often with a book in his hand that represents the constitution.

teile.einleitung: Florian of Lorch is a saint of the Christian Church. He lived about 1,700 years ago in the Roman Empire. Today he is known above all as the patron saint of firefighters.
wichtigste: Florian was a Roman official and a Christian.
He lived in the Roman province of Noricum, in the area of present-day Austria.
He died in the year 304 as a martyr near Lauriacum, present-day Lorch on the Enns.
Saint Florian is said to protect against fire.
He is the patron saint of firefighters.
His feast day is 4 May.

abschnitte.text: Florian lived in the 3rd and early 4th century. He was an **official** in the service of the Roman administration in the province of **Noricum**. At this time Christians were being persecuted in the Roman Empire. Florian openly declared his faith and wanted to support imprisoned Christians. For that reason he was arrested.

In the year 304 Florian was killed because of his faith. According to tradition, he was thrown into the river **Enns** near **Lauriacum**. A person who dies because of their faith is called a **martyr**. Later Florian was venerated by the Church as a saint. The monastery of **St Florian** near Linz is said to have arisen over his grave.

Saint Florian is said to protect against **fire**. In pictures he often wears the clothing of a Roman soldier. With a **bucket of water** he puts out a burning house. That is why he is the **patron saint** of firefighters. On many fire stations and old farmhouses you see a figure or picture of him.

The feast day of Saint Florian is **4 May**. Around this day many fire brigades in Austria, southern Germany and Switzerland hold a service or a festival. Florian is also the patron saint of the Austrian province of Upper Austria. He is also invoked against floods and drought.

gewusst: From Saint Florian comes the “Saint Florian principle”: it describes when someone wants to keep a problem away from themselves only and prefers to push it on to others.
The first name Florian comes from the Latin word for “blooming”.

teile.einleitung: Fundamentalism describes an attitude that holds strictly and literally to the foundations of a faith. The term arose at the beginning of the 20th century among conservative Protestants in the USA. Today it is applied to movements in many religions.
wichtigste: The term goes back to the series of pamphlets “The Fundamentals” of 1910 to 1915.
The journalist Curtis Lee Laws coined the label “fundamentalist” in 1920.
Central to Protestant fundamentalism is the doctrine that the Bible is without error.
The Scopes trial of 1925 was about the teaching of evolution in schools.
Since the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979, people also speak of Islamic fundamentalism.
The sociology of religion interprets fundamentalism as a modern reaction to modernity.

abschnitte.text: Between **1910 and 1915**, the series of pamphlets **“The Fundamentals”** appeared in the USA. In them conservative Protestants defended the foundations of the Christian faith against **liberal theology**. In 1920 the Baptist journalist **Curtis Lee Laws** called those who were ready to fight for these foundations fundamentalists. So the term was at first a **self-description**.

For Protestant fundamentalism, the **inerrancy of the Bible** is central. The Bible is held to be correct in all its statements, including on questions of history and nature. Fundamentalists reject the **historical-critical interpretation**, which studies the Bible as a text from a particular time. Many hold **creationism**: they understand the creation story as a literal account. Young-Earth creationists consider the Earth to be only a few thousand years old, while natural science reckons with about 4.6 billion years.

In 1925 the teacher **John Scopes** was put on trial in the US state of **Tennessee**. He had taught the **theory of evolution**, although a law forbade this in state schools. The trial was followed all over the USA. To this day it counts as a symbol of the conflict between fundamentalism and modern science.

In 1979 a Shiite theocracy arose in Iran with the **Islamic Revolution** under Ayatollah Khomeini. Afterwards Western media transferred the term fundamentalism to Islamic movements. From 1987 to 1995, the **Fundamentalism Project** under Martin E. Marty and R. Scott Appleby compared such movements in Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism and other religions. Some experts, however, find the term imprecise for other religions.

The sociologist of religion **Martin Riesebrodt** and others interpret fundamentalism as a **modern reaction to modernity**. So it is not simply a holding on to old tradition. It is a protest movement against **secularisation**, that is, the decline of religion in public life, and against the diversity of opinions. In doing so, fundamentalist groups themselves use modern means such as the mass media.

gewusst: The word fundamentalism comes from the Latin “fundamentum”, which means “foundation”.
The Fundamentalism Project published its results in several thick volumes.

teile.einleitung: The Guru Granth Sahib is the holy scripture of the Sikhs. For them the book is not only a text, but their eternal guru, that is, their teacher. It is treated with great reverence.
wichtigste: The Guru Granth Sahib is the holy scripture of the Sikhs.
Guru Arjan compiled the first version, the Adi Granth, in 1604.
In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh declared the scripture the eternal guru.
The scripture is written in Gurmukhi.
The standard edition has 1,430 pages, called angs.
It also contains songs by Hindu and Muslim saints.

abschnitte.titel: From the Adi Granth to the eternal guru
abschnitte.text: The fifth guru, **Guru Arjan**, collected the hymns of the gurus in one book in 1604. It was called the **Adi Granth**, which means “first book”. Later hymns by Guru Tegh Bahadur were added. The tenth guru, **Guru Gobind Singh**, decided before his death in 1708 that after him no human being should be guru any more. Since then the scripture has been regarded as the **eternal guru** of the Sikhs.

The Guru Granth Sahib is written in the **Gurmukhi** script. It is used mainly for the Punjabi language. The standard edition has **1,430 pages**, which are called **angs**. All editions have the same page layout, so every passage can be found again everywhere. The texts are songs and poems that are sung.

Besides the hymns of the Sikh gurus, the book also contains songs by other saints. These include, for example, **Kabir** and **Baba Farid**. They came from Hindu and Muslim traditions. This shows an important idea of the Sikhs: truth about God is not tied to any one origin.

Every morning the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at a random place. The first passage there is read aloud and counts as guidance for the day, the **hukamnama**. During the reading, a whisk of animal hair, the **chaur**, is waved over the scripture. In the past this was a sign of honour for kings. In an **akhand path**, several people take turns reading the whole book without a break, which takes about 48 hours.

gewusst: In the gurdwara the scripture lies under a canopy on a raised place, like a king on a throne.
A large part of the hymns comes from Guru Arjan himself.

t80jc0v.t: Religion within the Bounds of Bare Reason

teile.einleitung: “Religion within the Bounds of Bare Reason” is a book by the philosopher **Immanuel Kant** from 1793. In it Kant asks what a reasonable person can accept about religion from their own insight. For him, the core of religion is good, moral action.
wichtigste: The book appeared in 1793.
The first part deals with radical evil in human nature.
For Kant, religion is the recognition of all our duties as divine commands.
Worship that tries to please God only through rituals Kant calls sham service.
For Kant, God is a postulate of practical reason.
In 1794 Kant received a royal reprimand and was no longer allowed to write about religion.

abschnitte.text: Immanuel Kant lived from 1724 to 1804 in **Königsberg** in Prussia. He is one of the most important thinkers of the **Enlightenment**. His work on religion consists of four parts, which he calls “pieces”. In them he examines Christian teachings such as sin, redemption and the Church. In each case he asks what reasonable, moral sense lies in them.

The first part deals with **radical evil**. By this Kant means a tendency in human beings to put their own wishes above the moral law. “Radical” here means that it reaches to the root, Latin “radix”. Even so, human beings remain free and responsible. They can turn to the good at any time. The later parts deal with the struggle between good and evil and with a community of good people.

Kant defines religion as **the recognition of all our duties as divine commands**. So one pleases God by living a good life. Anyone who thinks they satisfy God mainly through rituals, formulas or sacrifices is, according to Kant, engaged in a **sham service**. The German word “After” used to mean “false” or “not genuine”. Churches and customs can help, but are not the most important thing.

Already in the “Critique of Pure Reason” of 1781, Kant showed that God’s existence cannot be proved. Against the **ontological argument** he said: **being is not a real predicate**, that is, not a property like big or good. In practical philosophy, God becomes for Kant a **postulate of practical reason**. That is: anyone who acts morally may reasonably hope that there is a God who joins happiness and virtue.

The Prussian government did not like the book. In 1794 Kant received a sharp reprimand from King **Frederick William II**. He promised not to speak publicly about religion any more. After the king’s death in 1797, Kant no longer felt bound by the promise. The story shows how controversial free thought about religion was at that time.

gewusst: Kant almost never left his home town of Königsberg and yet made world history.
The title already states the programme: religion should only count as far as reason can justify it.

teile.einleitung: Baruch de Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher of the 17th century. He equated God with nature and demanded freedom of thought. His ideas were highly controversial at the time and later influenced many thinkers.
wichtigste: Spinoza was born in Amsterdam in 1632.
In 1656 he was expelled from the Jewish community.
His famous formula is “Deus sive natura”.
His “Ethics” is built up using the geometrical method.
He earned money as a lens grinder.
The “Tractatus theologico-politicus” appeared anonymously in 1670.
Albert Einstein said in 1929 that he believed in “Spinoza’s God”.

abschnitte.text: Spinoza was born in 1632 in **Amsterdam** into a Portuguese-Jewish family. In 1656 the community placed him under a ban, the **cherem**. The reason was his views, which were regarded as heretical. After that he lived modestly and independently. He earned part of his living as a **lens grinder** for microscopes and telescopes.

Spinoza’s central idea is summed up in the formula **“Deus sive natura”**, which means “God or nature”. For him, God is the one infinite **substance**, which is identical with nature. God is therefore not outside the world, but is everything that is. Such a teaching is called **pantheism**. The word “pantheist” was first used by the Irish freethinker John Toland in 1705.

His main work is called **“Ethics”**. It has the subtitle “ordine geometrico demonstrata”, that is, proved by the geometrical method. As in mathematics, Spinoza derives **propositions** with proofs from definitions and axioms. In 1670 his **“Tractatus theologico-politicus”** appeared anonymously. In it he demanded freedom of thought and speech and read the Bible as a historical document, and the book was soon banned.

In Germany, Spinoza became well known again through the **Pantheism Controversy** of 1785. Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi claimed that **Gotthold Ephraim Lessing** had declared himself a Spinozist before his death. Moses Mendelssohn disagreed. In 1929 **Albert Einstein** wrote to a rabbi that he believed in Spinoza’s God, who reveals himself in the harmony of the world. He did not believe in a God who concerns himself with the fates of individuals.

gewusst: Spinoza’s “Ethics” was only published after his death, in 1677.
Einstein, who lived and worked in Bern for some years, referred to Spinoza when people asked him about his beliefs.

teile.einleitung: Hermes is a god of the Greek myths. He was the swift messenger of the gods and protected travellers and traders. For the Romans he was called Mercury.
wichtigste: Hermes was the messenger of the gods for the Greeks.
He delivered above all the messages of Zeus.
He wore winged shoes and a hat with wings.
In his hand he held a staff with two snakes.
He protected travellers and traders.
For the Romans he was called Mercury.

abschnitte.text: In the Greek myths **Hermes** is the **messenger of the gods**. He delivered the messages of the gods, above all of **Zeus**, his father. Hermes was very swift. On his feet he wore **sandals with wings**, with which he could fly through the air. On his head he often wore a flat **travelling hat with small wings**.

According to the myth, Hermes was a clever rascal even as a baby. On the day of his birth he stole the **cattle** of his brother **Apollo**. So that nobody would find the trail, he made the animals walk backwards. From a **tortoise shell** he built a **lyre**, a stringed instrument. Apollo liked the music so much that he let Hermes keep the cattle in exchange for the lyre.

In his hand Hermes often holds a staff, the **kerykeion**. **Two snakes** wind around it, and at the top it often has small wings. The staff was a sign for messengers and heralds. They were allowed to travel unhindered through foreign territory. According to the myth, Hermes also accompanied the souls of the dead into the underworld.

Hermes was the god of **roads**, of **trade** and of travellers. That is why merchants and walkers prayed to him. By the roadside in Greece there were stone pillars for Hermes. For the **Romans** the messenger of the gods was called **Mercury**. He too was responsible for traders and travellers.

gewusst: The planet Mercury is named after the Roman messenger of the gods; it orbits the sun the fastest.
The staff of Hermes often appears today in logos of trade and the post.

teile.einleitung: **Ethics** is a part of philosophy. It asks what **good and right action** is and how we can live well together. All people face such questions, whether in the family, at school or in politics.
wichtigste: Ethics examines what good and right action is.
Morality means the rules and values by which people act.
A good trait of character such as courage or honesty is called a virtue.
Conscience is the inner voice that tells us what is good or bad.
A dilemma is a situation in which you have to choose between two bad options.
Aristotle wrote the “Nicomachean Ethics”, and Immanuel Kant formulated the categorical imperative.
Utilitarianism asks about the consequences of an action for the happiness of as many people as possible.

abschnitte.text: The two words are often confused. **Morality** means the **rules and values** by which people in a community act, for example: you should not lie. **Ethics** thinks about these rules. It asks: why does a rule apply? Is it fair? What should you do when two rules contradict each other?

The Greek philosopher **Aristotle** wrote the **“Nicomachean Ethics”**. He asked how a person leads a good and happy life. His answer: through **virtues**. These are good traits of character such as **courage**, **honesty** or **justice**. You learn virtues through practice. Someone who often acts bravely becomes a brave person in time.

The philosopher **Immanuel Kant** formulated the **categorical imperative**. Put simply, it says: act only in a way that could also be a rule for everyone. For Kant what counts above all is whether an action is right because it is done out of duty. **Utilitarianism**, by contrast, looks at the **consequences**. What is right is what increases the **happiness of as many people as possible**. Both views help with thinking, but sometimes lead to different answers.

**Conscience** is the inner voice that tells us whether something is good or bad. Even so, the decision is sometimes hard. In a **dilemma** you have to choose between two options that both have drawbacks. An example: you promised a friend to keep a secret, but the secret could harm someone. At school, such questions are discussed, for example, in the subject Ethics, Religions, Community.

gewusst: The word ethics comes from the Greek “ethos”, which means custom or habit.
In Switzerland, cantonal ethics committees examine research projects in which people take part.

teile.einleitung: Hasidism is a religious movement within Judaism. It arose in the 18th century in Eastern Europe and stresses joy, prayer and a close bond with a spiritual leader, the rebbe.
wichtigste: Hasidism arose in the 18th century in Eastern Europe.
The spiritual leader is called a rebbe or tzaddik.
The opponents of the Hasidim were called Mitnagdim.
The Vilna Gaon led the resistance from Lithuania.
Chabad-Lubavitch goes back to Shneur Zalman of Liadi and has centres all over the world.

abschnitte.text: **Hasidism** arose in the **18th century** in Eastern Europe. Its founder is regarded as **Israel ben Eliezer**, known as the **Baal Shem Tov**. The movement stresses that one can serve God with **joy**, sincere **prayer**, singing and dancing. This appealed to many ordinary people. At the centre of a community stands the **rebbe**, also called a **tzaddik**. He is seen as an intermediary between God and his followers, and many groups have rebbe dynasties.

Not everyone was enthusiastic. The opponents were called **Mitnagdim**, which means “opponents”. They stressed thorough study of the **Talmud** and rejected the reverence for the rebbes. Their most important leader was **Elijah ben Solomon**, the **Vilna Gaon**. He pronounced bans against the Hasidim. **Lithuania** thus became a centre of the Mitnagdim.

A well-known Hasidic movement is **Chabad-Lubavitch**. It goes back to **Shneur Zalman of Liadi**, who wrote the basic work “**Tanya**”. Chabad is now known for its **community centres all over the world**. There are such centres in **Switzerland** too. They offer services, lessons and festivals.

gewusst: Many Hasidic men still wear clothing that recalls the fashion of Eastern Europe about 200 years ago.
The name Chabad is formed from the initial letters of the Hebrew words for wisdom, understanding and knowledge.

teile.einleitung: A cardinal is a high dignitary of the Roman Catholic Church. Cardinals advise the pope and elect a new one after his death or resignation. You recognise them by their red clothing.
wichtigste: Cardinals are the highest dignitaries after the pope.
They are appointed by the pope.
They wear red clothing and a red skullcap.
Red recalls loyalty to the point of blood.
Cardinals under 80 elect the new pope in the conclave.

abschnitte.text: Cardinals wear **red clothing** and a red skullcap on the head. On solemn occasions they also wear a square red cap, the **biretta**. The red colour has a special meaning. It recalls **loyalty to the point of blood**. A cardinal is meant to be ready to give everything for his faith and the Church.

Cardinals are appointed by the **pope**. Many of them are bishops of large cities, others head offices in the Vatican. Together they form the **College of Cardinals**. They advise the pope on important questions. Bishops from Switzerland too have been appointed cardinals.

When a pope dies or resigns, the cardinals elect a successor. Only cardinals under **80 years old** may vote. The election is called a **conclave** and takes place in the **Sistine Chapel** in the Vatican. After each round of voting, the ballot papers are burned. When **white smoke** rises from the chimney, a new pope has been elected.

gewusst: Conclave means “with a key”, because the cardinals are locked in during the election.
Black smoke over the Sistine Chapel shows that no pope has yet been elected.

teile.einleitung: Ganesha is one of the most popular gods in Hinduism. You recognise him at once by his elephant head. He is regarded as the god who removes obstacles, and as the god of wisdom.
wichtigste: Ganesha has a human body and an elephant head.
He rides on a small mouse.
He is said to remove obstacles and grant a good start.
His father is the god Shiva, his mother the goddess Parvati.
He is regarded as the god of wisdom and cleverness.
He especially likes to eat sweet things.

abschnitte.text: Ganesha has a **human body** and an **elephant head**. He often has a round belly and four arms. In most pictures he has only one whole **tusk**; the other is broken off. In his hands he holds various objects, often a **sweet** as well. Ganesha can be seen in pictures, figures and temples in India and many other countries.

Ganesha is the son of the god **Shiva** and the goddess **Parvati**. Shiva is one of the most important gods of the Hindus. According to a well-known story, Parvati formed Ganesha herself and set him as a guard before her door. In a quarrel Ganesha lost his head. Shiva then gave him the head of an elephant, and so Ganesha came back to life.

Ganesha is regarded as the god who removes **obstacles** from the way. That is why many Hindus pray to him first when they begin something new. It may be a journey, an exam, a festival or a new business. Ganesha is also the god of **wisdom** and **cleverness**. That is why schoolchildren and learners especially like him.

Ganesha rides on a small **mouse**. The great god and the small animal belong together. The mouse gets through every crack, just as Ganesha overcomes every obstacle. Ganesha loves sweet things, especially sweet balls and dumplings called **modak**. At the great festival of **Ganesh Chaturthi**, many sweets are offered to him.

gewusst: According to a legend, Ganesha used his broken tusk to write down the great Indian epic Mahabharata.
At the festival of Ganesh Chaturthi, Ganesha figures are often brought ceremonially into the water at the end.

teile.einleitung: The **disenchantment of the world** is a concept of the German sociologist **Max Weber** (1864 to 1920). It describes how people in the modern age explain the world less and less with mysterious forces and more and more with science and calculation. Weber saw in this part of a great process of rationalisation.
wichtigste: Weber made the concept especially well known in 1917 in his lecture “Science as a Vocation”.
Closely connected is the process of rationalisation.
“The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism” appeared in 1904 and 1905.
According to Weber, Calvin’s doctrine of predestination created an inner unease among believers.
He called the disciplined way of life in one’s job inner-worldly asceticism.
For the compelling order of the modern economy he used the image of the iron cage.

abschnitte.text: In his lecture **“Science as a Vocation”** of 1917, Weber explained the idea: modern people believe that in principle everything can be mastered by **calculation**. You no longer have to win over spirits by magic. That does not mean that everyone understands everything. But people trust that there is an explanation. This attitude belongs to **rationalisation**, that is, to the fact that life, the economy and the state are ordered more and more by rules and purposes.

In his essay **“The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism”** of 1904 and 1905, Weber asked how religion influences the economy. He looked especially at the teaching of the reformer **John Calvin** of Geneva. According to the **doctrine of predestination**, God has already determined beforehand who will be saved. Weber thought this troubled believers deeply. Many sought certainty in hard, honest work.

Weber called this way of life **inner-worldly asceticism**: you give up pleasure, live with discipline and work in a worldly job. Profits were not spent on luxury, but put back into the work. According to Weber, this attitude helped to shape modern capitalism. Later, however, the economy no longer needed religion. Its order forces all people into it like an **iron cage**.

Weber also described three forms of **legitimate authority**: the legal, the traditional and the **charismatic**. Charismatic authority rests on the extraordinary appeal of a person whom people follow. Weber also distinguished the social forms **church** and **sect**. A church takes in everyone, while you join a sect by choice. This distinction was shared by his friend, the theologian **Ernst Troeltsch**.

gewusst: Weber is regarded as one of the founding fathers of sociology.
His theses on the Protestant ethic are still discussed, and also criticised, in research today.

teile.einleitung: In **Curriculum 21**, **ERG** stands for **Ethics, Religions, Community** (Ethik, Religionen, Gemeinschaft). In this area pupils learn about values, about different religions and about living together. At the public school the lessons are meant for everyone, regardless of their own faith.
wichtigste: ERG means Ethics, Religions, Community.
In primary school, ERG belongs to the subject area Nature, People, Society.
ERG is taught neutrally, independent of any denomination.
Denominational religious instruction is usually given by the churches.
In the canton of Zurich the subject is called Religions, Cultures, Ethics at lower secondary level.
Curriculum 21 was developed for 21 cantons.

abschnitte.text: **Curriculum 21** (Lehrplan 21) was developed for the **21** German-speaking and multilingual **cantons** of Switzerland. It describes what children and young people are to learn in compulsory school. In primary school, ERG belongs to the large subject area **Nature, People, Society**, NMG for short. At lower secondary level there is a subject of its own. In the canton of **Zurich** it is called **Religions, Cultures, Ethics**.

At the public school, ERG is taught **independently of any denomination**. That means: the teacher does not promote any one religion. You learn about Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism and other world views. People without a religion also appear. So all children can take part, no matter what their family believes. This fits with the **freedom of belief and conscience** in the Federal Constitution.

Alongside this there is **denominational religious instruction**. It is usually given by the **churches** or religious communities themselves. There you get to know your own faith better, for example in preparation for **confirmation**. This instruction is voluntary. Depending on the canton, it takes place in school rooms or in the parish.

In the ethics part you think about right action, about justice, friendship or quarrels. In the community part the subject is living together in the class, the family and society. Every community shares certain **norms**, that is, rules and values. An important skill in the subject is to **understand other views with respect**. You may hold a different opinion and still listen.

gewusst: In French-speaking Switzerland and in Ticino, curricula of their own apply, not Curriculum 21.
Curriculum 21 was introduced gradually in the cantons from the school year 2015/16.

teile.einleitung: The Baha’i Faith is a religion that arose in Persia in the 19th century. Its founder is Baha’u’llah. Baha’is believe in one God and in the unity of all people.
wichtigste: The founder of the Baha’i religion is Baha’u’llah (1817 to 1892).
The religion arose in the middle of the 19th century in Persia, now Iran.
Its forerunner was the Bab, whose title means “The Gate”.
An important principle is the unity of humankind.
Every House of Worship has nine sides.
The New Year festival Naw-Ruz is around 21 March.

abschnitte.text: The Baha’i religion arose in the middle of the 19th century in **Persia**, now Iran. From 1844 a man known as the **Bab** announced a coming messenger of God. Bab is an Arabic word and means “gate”. He was executed in 1850. Baha’is see in **Baha’u’llah** (1817 to 1892) the messenger of God who had been announced.

Baha’is believe in one single God. They see the founders of great religions such as Abraham, Moses, Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad as messengers of the same God. The **unity of humankind** is especially important: all people are one family. The Baha’is also stress the **equality of men and women**, education for all and the harmony of science and religion.

Baha’is meet for prayer and devotion. A **House of Worship** always has **nine sides** and nine entrances. In the Baha’i Faith the number nine stands for perfection. The houses are open to all visitors, whatever their religion. The only one in Europe so far stands in **Langenhain** near Frankfurt am Main and was dedicated in 1964.

The Baha’is have a calendar of their own with **19 months** of 19 days each. Their New Year festival **Naw-Ruz** falls on the beginning of spring, around **21 March**. Before it, Baha’is fast during the day for 19 days. Another major festival is Ridvan. In Iran, Baha’is are still persecuted today; their world centre is in Haifa in Israel.

gewusst: Baha’is have no priests; the communities are led by elected councils.
The House of Worship in Langenhain is open to all people, not only to Baha’is.

teile.einleitung: In Hinduism, the god Vishnu comes down to earth again and again in a new form. These forms are called avatars. The best-known list counts ten avatars, from a fish to the future rider Kalki.
wichtigste: “Avatar” means the descent of a god.
The best-known list counts ten avatars, called the Dashavatara.
As the fish Matsya, Vishnu saved the first man, Manu, from a flood.
As the tortoise Kurma, he carried a mountain on his back.
Narasimha is half man, half lion.
Rama and Krishna are the most popular avatars.
Kalki is not expected to appear until the future.

abschnitte.text: **Vishnu** is one of the most important gods in Hinduism. He is regarded as the **preserver** of the world. Whenever evil gets the upper hand, he comes down to earth to restore order. Such a form is called an **avatar**, which means “descent”. The best-known list of the ten avatars is called the **Dashavatara**.

The first avatar is the fish **Matsya**. He warned the first man, **Manu**, of a great flood and pulled his boat to safety. As the tortoise **Kurma**, Vishnu supported a mountain with which gods and demons churned the **Ocean of Milk**. As the boar **Varaha**, he lifted the earth out of the primeval ocean. In this way the series begins with animal forms.

**Narasimha** is half man, half lion. He defeated the demon king **Hiranyakashipu** and protected his devout son Prahlada. After that Vishnu appeared as the dwarf **Vamana**. He asked the demon king **Bali** for as much land as he could measure out in three steps. Then he grew to a gigantic size and crossed the whole world in **three steps**.

**Rama** and **Krishna** are especially revered. Rama is the seventh avatar and the hero of the epic **Ramayana**. Krishna is the eighth avatar and speaks to the warrior Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita. The tenth avatar, **Kalki**, is not expected to appear until the future. According to belief, he will come at the end of the present age on a white horse and put an end to evil.

gewusst: The English word “avatar” for a character in a computer game comes from this Hindu concept.
In some lists, the Buddha is also counted as one of the ten avatars of Vishnu.

teile.einleitung: Jainism is an ancient religion from India. Its most important commandment is to harm no living being. The aim of the Jains is to free the soul from karma.
wichtigste: Jainism arose in India and is very old.
The most important teacher is regarded as Mahavira, who lived at the time of the Buddha.
The highest commandment is called ahimsa: to harm no living being.
The three jewels are right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.
The monks divide into Digambaras and Shvetambaras.
The most important festival is called Paryushana.
The aim is liberation from the cycle of rebirths.

abschnitte.text: **Jainism** is a religion from India. Its followers are called **Jains**. The most important teacher is regarded as **Mahavira**, who lived at about the same time as the Buddha. The highest commandment is **ahimsa**, which means: do no violence to any living being. This applies to people, animals and even the smallest creatures.

The way to liberation is described by the **three jewels**: right faith, right knowledge and right conduct. Right conduct means right action in everyday life. Jains believe in **rebirth**. Every deed leaves karma, which clings to the soul. When the soul is cleansed of all karma, it is freed. This liberation is called **moksha**.

abschnitte.titel: Monks with broom and mouth cloth
abschnitte.text: Among the monks there are two large groups. **Digambara** means “sky-clad”; these monks wear no clothes. **Shvetambara** means “white-clad”. Some monks wear a **cloth in front of the mouth**, so that they do not breathe in small insects. With a soft **broom** they gently sweep animals aside before they walk or sit down.

Many Jains live strictly vegetarian. The strictly devout also do not eat **root vegetables** such as onions, garlic or potatoes. When these are dug up, many tiny creatures in the soil die, and the whole plant is killed. Some eat only in daylight, so that they do not overlook any insects. In this way ahimsa shows itself at the dining table too.

An important teaching is called **anekantavada**, the “doctrine of many-sidedness”. It says that no human being sees the whole truth. That is why you should respect other views. The most important festival of the year is **Paryushana**. It lasts eight to ten days, with fasting and reflection. At the end, Jains ask others for forgiveness for all the mistakes of the past year.

gewusst: Some Jain monks sweep the ground before they sit down, so as not to tread on an ant.
The Jains are a small religion, but have built many well-known temples in India.

teile.einleitung: The **Digambara** are one of the two major branches of **Jainism**, an ancient religion from India. Their name means “sky-clad”. Their monks give up every possession, even clothes.
wichtigste: Digambara means “sky-clad”.
The monks own almost nothing; typical are a peacock-feather whisk and a water vessel.
The other major branch of Jainism is called Shvetambara, “white-clad”.
According to traditional Digambara teaching, women must first be reborn as men in order to be liberated.
The great statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola stands in the state of Karnataka.

abschnitte.text: Jainism goes back to **Mahavira**, who lived in ancient India. An important principle is **ahimsa**, not harming any living being. In time, the Jains split into two branches. The **Shvetambara** wear white clothes. The **Digambara** live especially strictly. They are found mainly in the south and centre of India.

Digambara monks wear no clothes. For them this is a sign of complete **non-possession**. They own only a **peacock-feather whisk** and a **water vessel**. With the soft feathers they gently brush small animals away before they sit down, so that they do not harm any living beings. They need the water for cleansing. According to their teaching, complete renunciation is necessary for liberation. Because women do not live like this, according to the traditional view they can only be liberated in a life as a man. The Shvetambara see this differently.

An important centre of the Digambara is **Shravanabelagola** in the state of **Karnataka**. There, on a hill, stands the huge statue of **Bahubali**, also called Gommateshvara. It is about 17 metres high and carved from a single block of rock. About every twelve years it is anointed with milk, water and colours at the great festival of **Mahamastakabhisheka**. Then very many pilgrims come.

gewusst: The statue of Bahubali is among the largest free-standing statues made from a single stone in the world.
Digambara monks usually walk barefoot from place to place and eat only once a day.

teile.einleitung: Dharma is one of the most important concepts in Hinduism. It refers to the cosmic order and the duties that follow from it for every person. No single English word fully captures it.
wichtigste: Dharma means roughly order, law and duty.
Many Hindus call their religion Sanatana Dharma, “eternal order”.
Svadharma is one’s own personal duty.
The best-known law book of the Dharmashastra literature is the Manusmriti.
Varnashrama dharma sums up the duties according to social class and stage of life.
Grihastha is the stage of family and work, vanaprastha that of the forest hermit.

abschnitte.text: **Dharma** is a word from **Sanskrit**. It refers to the **cosmic order** that holds everything together. From this follow people’s **duties**: how to live rightly and well. That is why dharma is translated as **order, law and duty**. Many Hindus themselves call their religion **Sanatana Dharma**, the “eternal order”. The term “Hinduism”, by contrast, was coined from outside.

According to this teaching, every person has their own duty, the **svadharma**. It arises from their position in society and their stage of life. The **Bhagavad Gita**, a famous holy text, says: one’s own duty is better than someone else’s, even if one performs it imperfectly.

There are ancient texts that describe dharma in detail. They are called **Dharmashastra**. The best-known law book is the **Manusmriti**. It regulates the duties of the classes and stages of life. From early on it was **controversial**, because it lays down the caste order. The social reformer **B. R. Ambedkar** burned it in 1927 in protest.

The term **varnashrama dharma** sums up the duties according to **class** (varna) and **stage of life** (ashrama). Traditionally there are four stages of life. First you are a **student**. As a **grihastha** you found a family and work; many texts call this stage the foundation of all the others. After that you gradually withdraw as a **vanaprastha**, a forest hermit. Finally life as a **sannyasin** can follow, who renounces everything worldly.

gewusst: The word dharma also exists in Buddhism; there it mainly refers to the teaching of the Buddha.
The wheel in the middle of the Indian flag is connected with dharma.

teile.einleitung: The Avesta is the sacred collection of writings of Zoroastrianism. This religion goes back to the prophet Zarathustra in ancient Iran. The Avesta contains prayers, hymns and rules for a pure life.
wichtigste: The Avesta is the holy scripture of the Zoroastrians.
It is written in the ancient Iranian language Avestan.
The Gathas are regarded as the work of Zarathustra himself.
The Gathas are 17 hymns.
The Vendidad regulates purity and the warding off of demons.
The Zand is a commentary in Middle Persian.

abschnitte.text: The **Avesta** is the collection of holy texts of **Zoroastrianism**. This religion arose in ancient Iran and goes back to the prophet **Zarathustra**. The Zoroastrians worship one supreme god, Ahura Mazda. The Avesta contains prayers, hymns and rules for ritual purity. It is written in the ancient Iranian language **Avestan**.

The oldest part of the Avesta is the **Gathas**. They are 17 hymns in very archaic Old Avestan. They are attributed to **Zarathustra** himself. The Gathas are embedded in the liturgy of the **Yasna**, that is, the most important service. They deal with the struggle between good and evil and with people’s free choice.

Another part is called the **Vendidad** or Videvdad. The name means “law against the demons”. It regulates **ritual purity**, for example the right way of dealing with the dead. It can be understood as a kind of priestly law book. It is meant to help keep evil away.

The **Zand** is a commentary on the Avesta in Middle Persian, also called **Pahlavi**. It translates and explains the old texts. This is where the older name “Zend-Avesta” comes from. Today Zoroastrians live mainly in Iran and in India, where they are called **Parsis**. In their temples a sacred fire burns as a sign of purity.

gewusst: A large part of the original Avesta has been lost over time.
For a long time the texts were passed on only by word of mouth before they were written down.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland it is mainly the **cantons** that decide which public holidays apply. That is why days off are not the same everywhere. Important rules on this are in the federal **Employment Act** (Arbeitsgesetz).
wichtigste: The Employment Act in principle forbids employing workers on Sundays.
The cantons may treat at most eight public holidays like Sundays.
The national holiday on 1 August is treated like a Sunday all over Switzerland.
Since a popular vote in 1993, 1 August has been a day off nationwide.
Anyone who wants to be absent on a religious holiday not recognised by the canton must give notice at least three days in advance.
In Ticino and in Valais, Good Friday is not a general public holiday.

abschnitte.text: The **Employment Act** in principle forbids employing workers on **Sundays**. Exceptions are needed, for example, for hospitals, the railways or the police, and they require a permit. The cantons may in addition treat **at most eight public holidays** a year like Sundays. Each canton decides for itself which ones these are. Many cantons include, for example, New Year’s Day, Ascension Day and Christmas.

Under the Employment Act only one holiday is treated like a Sunday in **all of Switzerland**: the **national holiday on 1 August**. It recalls the Federal Charter of 1291. For a long time, however, 1 August was a normal working day in many places. Only after a **popular vote in 1993** did it become a day off nationwide. Since 1994 everyone has had this day off.

In cantons with a Catholic tradition, days such as Corpus Christi or All Saints’ Day are often days off. In cantons with a Reformed tradition, **Good Friday**, for example, counts as a high holiday. Good Friday is a day off in almost all cantons, but not in **Ticino** and **Valais**. St Stephen’s Day on 26 December and Berchtold’s Day on 2 January apply only in some cantons.

Not all religions have cantonal public holidays. That is why the Employment Act also protects other religious holidays. Anyone who does not want to work on a Jewish or Muslim holiday, for example, may be absent. But you must give notice **at least three days in advance**. The employer may require you to **make up the working time**, that is, work extra before or after. In addition, when asked, he must where possible grant **time off for religious celebrations**.

gewusst: 1 August was celebrated as a national day for the first time in 1891, for the 600th anniversary of the Federal Charter.
Because every canton has its own public holidays, you can work on one day in one canton and have the day off in the neighbouring canton.

teile.einleitung: An ashram is a place in India where people lead a spiritual life together and learn. They often live there with a teacher, a guru. In Hinduism the word also stands for the four stages of life.
wichtigste: An ashram is a place for spiritual life and learning.
An ashram is often led by a guru.
Daily life includes meditation, prayer and simple work.
Mahatma Gandhi founded the Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad.
Rishikesh on the Ganges is regarded as the “yoga capital of the world”.
In Hinduism the four stages of life are called ashramas.

abschnitte.text: In an **ashram**, people live together who are concerned with faith, meditation and wisdom. There is often a teacher, the **guru**. The day usually follows a simple routine: people meditate, pray, learn and help with the work, for example in the kitchen or the garden. Many ashrams lie quietly in nature. Some also take in guests who want to live there for a while.

The Indian freedom fighter **Mahatma Gandhi** founded the **Sabarmati Ashram** in Ahmedabad. He lived there from 1917. In the ashram his followers lived simply and, for example, spun cotton themselves. From here Gandhi set off in 1930 on the famous **Salt March**. With it he protested without violence against the British salt tax.

The town of **Rishikesh** lies at the foot of the Himalayas on the sacred river **Ganges**. There are a great many ashrams there. That is why Rishikesh is called the “yoga capital of the world”. In 1968 the British band **The Beatles** visited an ashram there. Since then even more people from all over the world have come to Rishikesh.

In Hinduism, the four stages of life are also called **ashramas**. The first stage is the time as a pupil, in which you learn. The second is life as a father or mother of a family with a home and a job, called **grihastha**. In the third stage you withdraw, in the past into the forest. The fourth is life as a wandering monk who gives up all possessions.

gewusst: The Beatles wrote many new songs during their stay in Rishikesh in 1968.
Gandhi’s Salt March began in 1930 at the Sabarmati Ashram.

teile.einleitung: Humanism puts human beings and their dignity at the centre. It arose as an educational movement in the Renaissance. Today many people without religion also call themselves humanists.
wichtigste: Humanism comes from the Latin “humanus”, human.
At the centre are human beings and their dignity.
Renaissance humanism began in the 14th century in Italy.
The motto “ad fontes” means “to the sources”.
Erasmus of Rotterdam lived for a long time in Basel and is buried in Basel Minster.
Today’s secular humanism relies on reason and human dignity.

abschnitte.text: **Humanism** began in the **14th century** in Italy, in the time of the **Renaissance**. Scholars rediscovered the texts of the ancient Greeks and Romans. Their motto was **“ad fontes”**, which means “to the sources”. They wanted to read the ancient **original texts** rather than only later interpretations. Education was to make people better and freer.

The most famous humanist was **Erasmus of Rotterdam**. He lived for many years in **Basel** and worked there with printers. In 1516 the **New Testament in Greek** appeared from the printer Johannes Froben, in the original text and with a Latin translation. Martin Luther later used it for his translation of the Bible. Erasmus died in Basel in 1536 and is buried in **Basel Minster**.

The Zurich reformer **Huldrych Zwingli** was also shaped by humanism. He read the writings of Erasmus with enthusiasm and visited him in Basel in 1516. The demand to read the Bible in the **original text** shaped his Reformation in Zurich. In this way humanism also influenced the history of Switzerland.

Today many people without religion call themselves **humanists**. People speak of **secular humanism**. Secular means: not religious. These humanists base their values on **reason**, science and **compassion**. **Human dignity** is for them the most important standard. Many religious people also share humanist values.

At a **humanist Gymnasium** (an academic secondary school), **Latin and Greek** traditionally stand at the centre. The ancient languages are cultivated because the humanists wanted to read the ancient texts in the original. In Switzerland, at many Gymnasiums you can choose Latin or Greek as a focus.

gewusst: Erasmus wrote almost all his works in Latin, the common language of the scholars of Europe.
The Italian poet Francesco Petrarch is often regarded as the father of humanism.

teile.einleitung: Grave goods are things that are placed in the grave with the dead. They show what people believed about death and a life afterwards. Especially famous are the rich tombs of ancient Egypt.
wichtigste: Grave goods are objects placed in the grave with the dead.
The ancient Egyptians believed in a life in the afterlife.
Food, furniture and jewellery were meant to help the dead person there.
Small servant figures are called ushabti, vessels for organs are called canopic jars.
The Book of the Dead contained spells for the journey into the afterlife.
Most pyramids were already robbed by tomb robbers in antiquity.
In 1922 Howard Carter found the almost untouched tomb of Tutankhamun.

abschnitte.text: For many thousands of years, people have placed things in the grave with their dead. These can be tools, weapons, jewellery, vessels or food. They are called **grave goods**. They show that people believed in a continued existence after death or wanted to honour the dead person. For researchers, the **archaeologists**, grave goods are very valuable, because they reveal a great deal about life in the past.

The great pyramids in Egypt were tombs for the kings, the **pharaohs**. The Egyptians believed that the dead person lives on in the **afterlife**. There he was to have everything he needed. That is why he was given food, clothes, furniture and precious jewellery. Next to the Pyramid of Khufu, a dismantled wooden boat more than 40 metres long was found in a pit in 1954.

abschnitte.titel: Ushabti, canopic jars and Book of the Dead
abschnitte.text: Many tombs contained small figures, the **ushabti**. They were to do the work for the dead person in the afterlife. In mummification, some organs were taken out and placed in special jars, the **canopic jars**. Often a scroll was also placed in the grave, the **Book of the Dead**. It contained sayings and spells that were to lead the dead person safely into the afterlife.

The treasures in the tombs attracted **tomb robbers**. Almost all pyramids were already robbed in antiquity. A great exception is the tomb of the young pharaoh **Tutankhamun** in the Valley of the Kings. Howard Carter discovered it in 1922. It was full of treasures, including the famous golden death mask.

In Switzerland too, archaeologists have found many old graves with grave goods. In them lay, for example, jewellery, vessels or weapons from the Bronze Age, the Celtic period or the early Middle Ages. Such finds can be seen in museums today. They show that the custom was widespread in many cultures.

gewusst: The wooden boat beside the Pyramid of Khufu was put back together from over a thousand individual pieces.
In the tomb of Tutankhamun there were even chariots and game boards.

teile.einleitung: Baha’u’llah is the founder of the Baha’i religion. He was born in Tehran in 1817 and spent a large part of his life in exile. For Baha’is he is a messenger of God for our time.
wichtigste: Baha’u’llah means “Glory of God”.
His birth name was Mirza Husayn Ali Nuri.
He was born in Tehran in 1817.
In 1863, in the Ridvan Garden near Baghdad, he declared his mission.
